families.title: The Kadison–Ringrose cohomology conjecture
families.headline: **295. The Kadison–Ringrose cohomology conjecture.** Proves that every bounded Hochschild cocycle of degree at least two on a complex von Neumann algebra, with coefficients in the algebra itself, has a bounded primitive. Equivalently, all higher bounded Hochschild cohomology groups vanish, resolving the Kadison–Ringrose conjecture. ([Lean](lean/docs/295.md))

clauses.clause: every bounded Hochschild cocycle of degree at least two
clauses.coveredBy: f : Cochain M (n + 2) and hf, challenge.lean:32-33; Cochain, lines 12-13
clauses.note: Cochain is ContinuousMultilinearMap ℂ (Fin n → M) M, i.e. bounded multilinear. Degree n + 2 ≥ 2. Cocycle: δf = 0 at every (n+3)-tuple. The differential (lines 15-24) is the standard Hochschild one: v0·f(v1,…) + Σ_j (−1)^(j+1) f(…, v_j·v_(j+1), …) + (−1)^(n+1) f(v0,…,v_(n−1))·v_n; mergeInputs (lines 15-18) merges positions j and j+1 correctly.

clauses.clause: on a complex von Neumann algebra
clauses.note: CStarAlgebra + WStarAlgebra (a C*-algebra with a predual: an abstract W*-algebra) is a fair encoding. But line 32 adds [TopologicalSpace.SeparableSpace M], and the only topology on a CStarAlgebra is its norm topology. A norm-separable W*-algebra is finite-dimensional: an infinite-dimensional one has an infinite family of mutually orthogonal nonzero projections p_k, and the projections Σ_{k∈S} p_k, S ⊆ ℕ, are pairwise at norm distance 1 — an uncountable discrete set. Covered only in finite dimensions.

clauses.clause: with coefficients in the algebra itself
clauses.coveredBy: Cochain M n takes values in M; differentialValue, lines 20-24
clauses.note: M as a bimodule over itself by left and right multiplication. Matches.

clauses.clause: has a bounded primitive
clauses.note: ∃ g : Cochain M (n + 1) with δg = f at every (n+2)-tuple; bounded because g is continuous multilinear. Matches.

clauses.clause: Equivalently, all higher bounded Hochschild cohomology groups vanish, resolving the Kadison–Ringrose conjecture
clauses.coveredBy: same as above, under the same restriction
clauses.note: For finite-dimensional W*-algebras (finite direct sums of matrix algebras) the vanishing of Hochschild cohomology in positive degrees is classical, so the stated theorem does not resolve the conjecture.

families.gap: The headline covers every complex von Neumann algebra. challenge.lean:32 adds [TopologicalSpace.SeparableSpace M]; in the norm topology this leaves only finite-dimensional W*-algebras, where the result is classical. The infinite-dimensional case — the whole content of the Kadison–Ringrose conjecture — is not stated.

families.title: Boolean functions violate the square-root degree bound by arbitrary factors
families.headline: **192. Boolean functions violate the square-root degree bound by arbitrary factors.** Disproves the proposed square-root bound relating a Boolean function's linear Fourier coefficients to its polynomial degree. For every C > 0, there is a sign-valued Boolean function f with $`\sum_i\widehat f(\{i\})\gt C\sqrt{\deg(f)}`$. Thus its total signed correlation with individual input bits can exceed the proposed bound by an arbitrary factor. ([Lean](lean/docs/192.md))

clauses.clause: Disproves the proposed square-root bound relating a Boolean function's linear Fourier coefficients to its polynomial degree
clauses.note: Stated over IsBoolean f, which is |f x| ≤ 1 (lines 34-35), not over ±1-valued f.

clauses.clause: For every C > 0, there is a sign-valued Boolean function f with Σ_i f̂({i}) > C√deg(f)
clauses.note: Quantifier order (∀ C > 0, ∃ n, ∃ f) matches. The Fourier coefficient as the uniform average of f·χ_s with Bool encoding signs (lines 16-28), the real Fourier degree as the largest |s| with f̂(s) ≠ 0 (lines 30-32) and the singleton sum (lines 40-41) are correct. 'Sign-valued' is weakened to [−1,1]-valued.

clauses.clause: Thus its total signed correlation with individual input bits can exceed the proposed bound by an arbitrary factor
clauses.note: Same weakening.

clauses.clause: (scope note) the ratio of the sum of the absolute values of those coefficients to √deg f is unbounded among positive-degree Boolean functions
clauses.note: Also over |f| ≤ 1. It follows from the first conjunct: nonconstancy forces deg f > 0, and Σ|f̂({i})| ≥ Σ f̂({i}).

families.gap: 'Sign-valued' is lost: IsBoolean (challenge.lean:34-35) asks only |f x| ≤ 1, so f may be any [−1,1]-valued function. For such f the violation is elementary: for odd d and S = Σ_i x_i, f = ±T_d(S/n) (Chebyshev) is bounded by 1, has real degree d once n ≥ d, and Σ_i f̂({i}) = E[f·S] = d + O(d³/n), so the ratio to √d grows like √d. The ±1-valued claim, which is what disproves the Gopalan–Servedio bound, is not stated.
families.scopeNoteOnGap: silent — the note says "it gives a nonconstant Boolean function on a finite sign cube" and "positive-degree Boolean functions", with no word that the values are relaxed to [−1,1]; the challenge file's comment (lines 5-8) concerns only the input encoding and the notion of degree.
families.asserts: For every C > 0 there are n > 0 and a nonconstant f : {±1}^n → ℝ with |f| ≤ 1 everywhere and C·√(deg f) < Σ_i f̂({i}); and Σ_i |f̂({i})| / √(deg f) is unbounded above over [−1,1]-valued f of positive real degree.

The name IsBoolean does not declare the relaxation; its body (line 35) is the relaxation.
No junk: division by √deg occurs only where 0 < deg (line 52).

families.title: Cycle–clique Ramsey numbers
families.headline: **189. Cycle–clique Ramsey numbers.** Proves the Erdős–Faudree–Rousseau–Schelp conjecture: $`R(C_m,K_n)=(m-1)(n-1)+1`$ for every $`m\ge n\ge3`$, except $`R(C_3,K_3)=6`$. This is the exact threshold forcing a red m-cycle or a blue n-clique in every red–blue coloring of a complete graph. ([Lean](lean/docs/189.md))

clauses.note: Adds the hypothesis m ≤ 2 * n (line 24): only n ≤ m ≤ 2n is covered.

clauses.clause: except R(C_3,K_3)=6
clauses.coveredBy: (m, n) ≠ (3, 3) at line 24; second conjunct, line 26
clauses.note: Matches.

clauses.clause: This is the exact threshold forcing a red m-cycle or a blue n-clique in every red–blue coloring of a complete graph
clauses.note: Red = G, blue = Gᶜ on Fin N; copies by ⊑ (non-induced containment); cycleGraph m is the m-cycle for m ≥ 3. RamseyProperty is upward closed in N (restrict a graph on Fin N' to Fin N), so the sInf is the threshold. Matches.

families.title: Riesz transforms and rectifiability in higher codimension
families.headline: **081. Riesz transforms and rectifiability in higher codimension.** Resolves the remaining higher-codimension Riesz-transform rectifiability problem: for d ≥ 4 and $`2\le n\le d-2`$, an n-Ahlfors–David regular Radon measure on ℝd is uniformly n-rectifiable whenever its n-dimensional Riesz transform is uniformly L2-bounded over all positive hard truncations. The rectifiability bounds depend only on dimension, regularity and operator bounds. ([Lean](lean/docs/081.md))

clauses.clause: for d ≥ 4 and 2 ≤ n ≤ d−2
clauses.note: 4 ≤ d, 2 ≤ n and n + 2 = d: only codimension exactly two (n = d − 2). For d ≥ 5 the values n = 2 … d − 3 are missing.

clauses.clause: an n-Ahlfors–David regular Radon measure on ℝ^d
clauses.note: r^n / C ≤ μ(B(x,r)) ≤ C r^n at every support point x and admissible radius 0 < r ≤ ediam(supp μ). Matches.

clauses.clause: is uniformly n-rectifiable
clauses.note: Big pieces of Lipschitz images: an M-Lipschitz g on the r-ball of ℝ^n with μ(B(x,r) ∩ range g) ≥ θ r^n. Equivalent to uniform rectifiability for ADR measures (David–Semmes); the scope note names this form.

clauses.clause: whenever its n-dimensional Riesz transform is uniformly L²-bounded over all positive hard truncations
clauses.note: Kernel (x−y)/|x−y|^(n+1); truncation ε < |x−y|; one bound C_R for every ε > 0 and every f ∈ L²(μ). Matches.

clauses.clause: The rectifiability bounds depend only on dimension, regularity and operator bounds
clauses.note: ∃ θ, M after d, n, C_AD, C_R and before ∀ μ. Matches.

families.title: A counterexample to periodic tiling in dimension three
families.headline: **155. A counterexample to periodic tiling in dimension three.** Constructs a finite translational tile in ℤ<sup>3</sup> that tiles space but admits no fully periodic tiling, disproving the periodic tiling conjecture in the smallest possible lattice dimension. Its unit-cube thickening gives the same counterexample in ℝ<sup>3</sup>, even with arbitrary real translation vectors. ([Lean](lean/docs/155.md))

clauses.note: T is a nonempty Finset and, for some A, (t, a) ↦ t + a is a bijection T × A → ℤ³. Matches.

clauses.clause: but admits no fully periodic tiling
clauses.note: No tiling complement A is invariant under a finite-index subgroup. Matches.

clauses.clause: disproving the periodic tiling conjecture in the smallest possible lattice dimension
clauses.note: IsLeast {d | …} 3 also asserts that d = 0, 1, 2 have no such tile. Matches.

clauses.clause: Its unit-cube thickening gives the same counterexample in ℝ³
clauses.note: T + [0,1]³ tiles ℝ³ almost everywhere for some A. The existence half matches.

clauses.clause: even with arbitrary real translation vectors
clauses.note: The ℝ³ non-periodicity is stated only for A ⊆ Set.range castLattice, i.e. integer translates. Not covered.

families.gap: The ℝ³ non-periodicity (lines 57-58) is asserted only for translation sets A ⊆ ℤ³ (A ⊆ Set.range castLattice). Tilings of the thickened tile by non-integer translates — which the headline explicitly includes with 'even with arbitrary real translation vectors' — are never quantified over, and what remains of the ℝ³ claim is close to a restatement of the ℤ³ claim.

families.title: Borsuk's conjecture fails in dimension nine
families.headline: **156. Borsuk's conjecture fails in dimension nine.** Constructs a compact subset of ℝ<sup>9</sup> that cannot be covered by ten sets of strictly smaller diameter, disproving Borsuk's covering assertion already in dimension nine. The example consists of rank-one orthogonal projectors onto lines in ℝ<sup>4</sup>, with the Frobenius metric. ([Lean](lean/docs/156.md))

families.title: Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture
families.headline: **173. Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture.** Proves Seymour's second-neighborhood conjecture: every nonempty finite oriented graph has a vertex with at least as many vertices at directed distance exactly two as at directed distance one. Oriented graphs may be arbitrary apart from the exclusion of loops and oppositely directed edge pairs. ([Lean](lean/docs/173.md))

families.title: The hot spots conjecture for simply connected planar domains
families.headline: **369. The hot spots conjecture for simply connected planar domains.** Proves a strict form of Burdzy's simply connected hot spots conjecture. On every smooth bounded simply connected planar domain, each nonzero eigenfunction for the first positive Neumann eigenvalue has no interior critical point, so all global extrema lie on the boundary. Eigenvalue multiplicity is allowed. ([Lean](lean/docs/369.md))

clauses.note: Nonempty, open, bounded, smooth boundary — and Convex ℝ Ω. Convexity stands in place of simple connectivity.

clauses.coveredBy: InFirstNeumannEigenspace, lines 38-43; rayleighValues and firstPositiveNeumannValue, lines 30-36; hne, line 51
clauses.note: Weak Neumann identity against every H¹ pair, with μ = inf of the Rayleigh quotient over mean-zero H¹; u is C^∞ up to the boundary, has mean zero, and is nonzero somewhere. Matches up to encoding.

clauses.clause: has no interior critical point
clauses.note: ∇u(x) ≠ 0 for all x ∈ Ω. Matches.

clauses.clause: so all global extrema lie on the boundary
clauses.note: Strict: inf of u over ∂Ω < u(x) < sup of u over ∂Ω for every x ∈ Ω. Matches.

clauses.clause: Eigenvalue multiplicity is allowed
clauses.note: Matches.
